title: Elijah, come soon
hookLine: after Havdalah, a song for Elijah, who is to announce redemption

lines: A MAN WHOSE DEATH IS NEVER RECORDED.
cards: The Havdalah candle is dipped into the spilled wine, and it goes out with a hiss. The room is darker now. Shabbat is over.
And then the room starts singing about a man whose death the Bible never records. Eliyahu hanavi. Elijah the prophet.
It's the same Elijah we met on Mount Carmel, calling down fire in the afternoon. But here he's not a figure from a story. He's someone the song asks to show up, soon, maybe this very week.

teach.b: First, why no death? In the book of Kings, Elijah doesn't die the way others do.

He's walking with his student Elisha, and a chariot of fire and horses of fire come between them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. The text never records his death. So in Jewish tradition, he's still around.

The closing verses of the prophets in the Hebrew Bible, in Malachi, say, in the old Jewish translation: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and terrible day of the LORD."

And he will turn the hearts of parents to children, and the hearts of children to their parents. So in Jewish tradition Elijah becomes the one who announces redemption, the herald who comes before the messiah.
The song is simple. Elijah the prophet, Elijah the Tishbite, Elijah the Gileadite. May he come to us soon, in our days, with the messiah, son of David.
Why sing it on Saturday night?

There's a tradition, built on a discussion in the Talmud, that Elijah won't arrive on Shabbat itself. Once Shabbat ends, the door is open again. So the song is a kind of hope at the start of the week: maybe this week.
Elijah shows up all over Jewish life. A cup is filled for him at the Passover seder, and the door is opened.

teach.h: A CUP, A CHAIR, A STRANGER.
teach.b: A chair is set for him at a baby boy's circumcision.
In folk stories he appears in disguise, a beggar, a stranger, to help someone in trouble.

how: Eliyahu HaNavi is sung at the end of Havdalah on Saturday night in many homes and synagogues; Elijah also has a cup at the Passover seder and a chair at a brit milah.

practice: Malachi says Elijah will turn the hearts of parents and children toward each other.
Think of one relationship where a heart could turn, and without planning anything, picture this week bringing one small turn: a call returned, a kind word, a door opened.
